key_points.base: Type I means we ship a change that does nothing, and Type II means we miss a real improvement. Which
points: Type I means we ship a change that does nothing, and Type II means we miss a real improvement.
Which is worse depends on cost.
For a risky lending policy a false positive can lose money, so I'd use a stricter alpha.
I'd control Type II by planning power and sample size before the test.
At p=0.08 after 7 days I wouldn't stop or keep extending until it crosses 0.05.
The stopping rule is fixed in advance, peeking inflates false positives, and sequential methods are the answer if early looks are needed.

key_points.base: I'd compute the sample size needed to detect the effect I care about. Detecting 0.1 percentage point
points: I'd compute the sample size needed to detect the effect I care about.
Detecting 0.1 percentage points on a 2% base rate needs a very large sample, so this test is probably underpowered.
Then I'd translate it into money: 0.1pp of default on the portfolio's average loan size can be expensive, so 'not significant' doesn't mean 'safe'.
I'd report a confidence interval for the difference.
Defaults mature after 90 days, so a 30-day window sees incomplete outcomes.
I'd use early proxies like delinquency, fixed-maturity cohorts, or survival analysis.

key_points.base: For example, segment A's overall approval rate looks lower than B's, but within every income band A
points: For example, segment A's overall approval rate looks lower than B's, but within every income band A is approved more often, because A has more applicants in the harder bands.
I'd detect it by always slicing key metrics by likely confounders and checking whether the direction flips.

For the board I'd report the stratified or adjusted comparison with a plain explanation, and say which question each number answers, because the aggregate answers a different question than the one they're asking.

key_points.base: I'd fix four inputs before starting: the baseline metric and its variance, the minimum detectable ef
points: I'd fix four inputs before starting: the baseline metric and its variance, the minimum detectable effect that would actually change a decision, the significance level (usually 5%), and the power (usually 80%).
Sample size grows with variance and with 1 over the MDE squared, so halving the effect needs about four times the users.
If we can't wait that long, I'd raise the MDE honestly, pick a less noisy metric, or use CUPED, which uses pre-experiment behavior as a covariate to cut variance.
I'd also commit to the sample size up front and not stop when the p-value first dips below 0.05.

key_points.base: I'd say: 'Our best estimate is X, and given the noise in our data, values from A to B are all plausi
points: I'd say: 'Our best estimate is X, and given the noise in our data, values from A to B are all plausible.

If we repeated this study many times, intervals built this way would capture the true value about 95% of the time.' Strictly, the true value is fixed, so 95% describes the procedure and not this particular interval.
Quadrupling the sample size roughly halves the width.
If they want one number, I give the estimate and always pair it with the range, and say what decision would change within that range.

key_points.base: With 20 independent tests at the 5% level, the chance of at least one false positive is 1 - 0.95^20,
points: With 20 independent tests at the 5% level, the chance of at least one false positive is 1 - 0.95^20, about 64%, so one p=0.04 is weak evidence.
I'd check whether this was a pre-declared primary metric.
If not, I'd treat it as a hypothesis to confirm in a follow-up test.

For the analysis I'd correct: Bonferroni or Holm control the chance of any false positive but cost power, while Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate and is better for exploratory work.
Going forward I'd pre-register one primary metric plus a few guardrail metrics.

key_points.base: Bootstrapping estimates the sampling distribution of any statistic, such as a median, a ratio or an
points: Bootstrapping estimates the sampling distribution of any statistic, such as a median, a ratio or an AUC, by resampling the data with replacement many times and recomputing it.
I'd use it when there's no clean analytical formula.
It breaks when observations aren't independent: resampling points of a time series destroys the autocorrelation, so I'd use a block bootstrap.
It also behaves badly for extreme statistics like the maximum, and for very small samples.
A thousand or more resamples is usually fine for a standard error, and more for stable tail percentiles.

key_points.base: Under a fair coin, 7 or more heads in 10 flips has probability about 17%, and the two-sided p-value
points: Under a fair coin, 7 or more heads in 10 flips has probability about 17%, and the two-sided p-value (7 or more, or 3 or fewer) is about 0.34, so there is no evidence of bias.
With 70 heads out of 100 the p-value is far below 0.001, which is strong evidence.
The p-value is the probability of data this extreme if the coin is fair, not the probability that the coin is fair.
I'd also report a confidence interval for the heads rate, which for 10 flips spans roughly 35% to 93%, to show how little 10 flips tell us.
One-sided versus two-sided should be chosen before seeing the data.

key_points.base: I'd say: individual users' spending is messy and skewed, but if you repeatedly take samples and aver
points: I'd say: individual users' spending is messy and skewed, but if you repeatedly take samples and average them, those averages form a bell shape centered on the true mean, with a spread that shrinks as samples grow.
That is why we can put a margin of error on an average and compare two groups with a standard test.
The common misconception is that the data itself becomes normal; it is the distribution of the average.
How large n must be depends on the skew: 30 is a rough rule for mild skew, but a metric dominated by rare big spenders may need thousands.
With a heavy-tailed metric I'd check with a bootstrap.

key_points.base: It depends on the decision. If we care about total revenue, the mean is the right quantity even thou
points: It depends on the decision.
If we care about total revenue, the mean is the right quantity even though it is noisy, since totals are mean times users.
If we care about a typical user's experience, the median or a trimmed mean is better.

For testing the mean, the central limit theorem usually still rescues a t-test at large n, but with heavy tails I'd confirm with a bootstrap interval or reduce variance with CUPED or winsorizing, stating what that does to the quantity being estimated.
Mann-Whitney tests whether one group tends to produce larger values, not specifically whether medians differ.
I'd report both mean and median with intervals.

key_points.base: No. p = 0.03 means that if A and B truly performed the same, data this extreme would show up about 3
points: p = 0.03 means that if A and B truly performed the same, data this extreme would show up about 3% of the time.
It is not the probability that B is better.

To answer the PM's actual question I'd fit a Bayesian model: put priors on each conversion rate (often weakly informative Beta priors), update with the data, and report P(B > A) from the posterior along with the expected lift and the expected loss if we choose wrong.
The answer depends on the prior, which should be stated and tested for sensitivity.
With lots of data and weak priors the two approaches usually agree closely.
I'd frame it for the PM in terms of decision risk.

key_points.base: A fixed-horizon p-value is only valid if you look once, at the pre-planned sample size. Stopping whe
points: A fixed-horizon p-value is only valid if you look once, at the pre-planned sample size.
Stopping when it first dips below 0.05 exploits random fluctuation: with daily looks over a few weeks, the real false-positive rate can reach 20 to 30%.

Options: pre-commit to a sample size and read results once; or use a sequential design such as group-sequential or alpha-spending boundaries, always-valid p-values, or a Bayesian stopping rule with calibrated thresholds.
If stakeholders need early reads, I'd allow monitoring for harm on guardrail metrics but not for declaring wins.
Novelty effects and day-of-week cycles are another reason to run full weeks.

key_points.base: First I'd learn how discounts were assigned: if marketing targeted engaged customers, or at-risk cus
points: First I'd learn how discounts were assigned: if marketing targeted engaged customers, or at-risk customers, the groups differ before treatment.
I'd map the likely causal structure, then compare like with like: propensity-score matching or weighting, or regression adjustment on pre-treatment covariates only.
If there is a rollout date, a region or an eligibility cutoff, difference-in-differences or regression discontinuity gives a stronger estimate.
I'd check covariate balance and run a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured factors.
Adjustment only handles what we measured, so I'd say so and recommend a small holdout experiment going forward.

key_points.base: With p1 and p2 as the arm rates, the standard error of the difference is sqrt(p1(1-p1)/n1 + p2(1-p2)
points: With p1 and p2 as the arm rates, the standard error of the difference is sqrt(p1(1-p1)/n1 + p2(1-p2)/n2), and the 95% interval is the difference plus or minus 1.96 times that.
For about 2% and 100,000 users per arm the standard error is roughly 0.063 percentage points, so differences under about 0.12 points are inside the noise.
The formula assumes independent users and a large enough n for the normal approximation, both fine here.
A common error is analyzing clicks or sessions while randomizing users, which understates variance; I'd analyze per user or use cluster-robust errors.
A bootstrap is a good cross-check.

key_points.base: It can mislead. A/B tests assume one user's outcome doesn't depend on anyone else's assignment. In a
points: It can mislead.
A/B tests assume one user's outcome doesn't depend on anyone else's assignment.
In a marketplace, treated buyers who grab limited inventory take it from control buyers, so the measured lift overstates what launching to everyone would deliver.
In social products, treated users influence their control friends, which shrinks the measured effect.
Better designs randomize at the level where the interaction happens: clusters of connected users, geographies or time-based switchbacks, accepting lower power.
I'd compare cluster-level and user-level estimates as a diagnostic and consider modelling the equilibrium effect.

key_points.base: Given a model with parameters, the likelihood is the probability it assigns to the data we saw. Maxi
points: Given a model with parameters, the likelihood is the probability it assigns to the data we saw.
Maximum likelihood chooses the parameters that maximize it.
For independent points the likelihood is a product, so we maximize the log, which turns it into a sum and avoids underflow.
Squared error is the negative log-likelihood of Gaussian noise, and cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of Bernoulli labels, so training those models is maximum likelihood.
It can fail with little data, where it overfits, and with perfectly separable classes, where logistic coefficients diverge; priors or regularization fix both.

key_points.base: Conversions are counts in a channel-by-outcome table, so a chi-square test of independence asks whet
points: Conversions are counts in a channel-by-outcome table, so a chi-square test of independence asks whether conversion rate depends on channel.
It needs independent users and reasonably large expected counts; otherwise use Fisher's exact test.
A significant result only says some channels differ.

To find which, I'd run pairwise comparisons with a correction such as Holm or Tukey rather than six uncorrected tests, and report effect sizes with intervals, since a huge sample makes tiny differences significant.
For revenue per user the analogue is ANOVA, or a rank-based test if the data are heavily skewed.

key_points.base: A bandit shifts traffic toward better-performing variants as evidence accumulates, which cuts the co
points: A bandit shifts traffic toward better-performing variants as evidence accumulates, which cuts the cost of showing a loser.
That fits headline testing, promotions and recommendations, where options are many, decisions are short-lived and the goal is reward, not a report.
An A/B test fits product changes where you need an unbiased estimate, a guardrail check and a decision you can defend.
With a bandit the unequal, adaptive allocation makes estimates for the weaker arms noisy and biased and complicates p-values.
Thompson sampling draws a plausible rate for each arm from its posterior and plays the best draw.
If the effect drifts, for example by day of week, a bandit can lock onto a stale winner unless it discounts old data.

key_points.base: Customers who are still active have an unknown churn time: we only know it is longer than what we ha
points: Customers who are still active have an unknown churn time: we only know it is longer than what we have observed.
Averaging observed lifetimes of churned customers biases the answer downward, and treating active customers as churned at today's date is also wrong.
Survival analysis handles this censoring.
A Kaplan-Meier curve estimates the share still subscribed at each tenure, and I would compare curves by plan or cohort.
To include features I'd use a Cox proportional hazards model, which gives hazard ratios, after checking that the proportionality assumption holds.
If the goal is a score for who will churn in the next 30 days, a classifier on a fixed window can be simpler.
